blocks.orig: Ruaha National Park is the second-largest national park during your Tanzania vacation after Nyerere National Park and located in central Tanzania. Due to its relative inaccessibility, it gets far fewer tourists than any comparable park in the Northern circuit. The Great Ruaha River flows through the park and is the most important river in the park.
blocks.html: Located in central Tanzania, Ruaha National Park is the second-largest park you can visit on a Tanzania holiday, surpassed only by Nyerere National Park. Because it is relatively hard to reach, visitor numbers are far lower than in any park of similar size on the Northern circuit. The Great Ruaha River runs through the park and is its most important waterway.

blocks.orig: Ruaha has a big variety of plants and trees. But it is mainly characterized by its acacias and the many baobab trees. There are over 1,650 plant species that have been identified.
blocks.html: Plant life in Ruaha is remarkably varied, yet the landscape is defined above all by acacias and the many baobab trees. More than 1,650 plant species have been recorded here.

blocks.orig: Ruaha has a huge population of African elephants. Some consider it to be the most concentrated population in Africa! The National Park is probably home to more elephants than any other parks in East Africa has. It is also home to great mammals like kudu, sable and roan antelopes which cannot be found in any other national park. It also has nearly 10% of Africa’s lion population living here! Other animals to spot here include leopards, cheetahs, giraffes. Many zebras, elands, impala, bat eared foxes and jackals live in the park. Despite the fact that no world-famous great migration takes place in this park, it is a beautiful park to visit. With a bit of luck, you may also see the endangered wild dogs in Ruaha National Park!
blocks.html: Ruaha holds an enormous number of African elephants; some people regard it as the densest elephant population anywhere in Africa! The park probably shelters more elephants than any other park in East Africa. It is also home to large mammals such as kudu, sable and roan antelope, which you won't find in any other national park, and close to 10% of all of Africa's lions live here as well! Leopards, cheetahs and giraffes can be spotted too, while zebras, elands, impala, bat-eared foxes and jackals roam the park in large numbers. No world-famous great migration passes through Ruaha, but it remains a wonderful park to explore. If luck is on your side, you might even catch sight of the endangered wild dogs in Ruaha National Park!

blocks.orig: Reptiles and amphibians in the National Park
blocks.html: Reptiles and amphibians in the park

blocks.orig: You can also find Reptiles and amphibians here! And crocodiles, poisonous and non-poisonous snakes, monitor and agama lizards and frogs live in and around the river. Ruaha National Park has an almost untouched and unexplored ecosystem. It will make your safari experience unique!
blocks.html: Reptiles and amphibians have their place here too. Crocodiles, venomous and harmless snakes, monitor and agama lizards and frogs all live in and along the river. The ecosystem of Ruaha National Park is still largely untouched and unexplored, which gives your safari a character all of its own!

blocks.orig: Not only is Ruaha the ideal place to watch elephants, but it is also a bird lover’s paradise! Around 571 different species of birds live in Ruaha National Park, including the Crested barbet, Dickinson’s kestrel, Pale-billed hornbill, Violet-crested turaco, Racket-tailed roller, Plovers, Kingfishers, Hornbills, Green-wood hoopoes, Sunbirds, Bee-eaters and Egrets.
blocks.html: Ruaha is not only the perfect spot for watching elephants; birders will feel in heaven here as well! Some 571 bird species have been counted in Ruaha National Park, among them the Crested barbet, Dickinson's kestrel, Pale-billed hornbill, Violet-crested turaco, Racket-tailed roller, Plovers, Kingfishers, Hornbills, Green-wood hoopoes, Sunbirds, Bee-eaters and Egrets.

blocks.html: Ruaha pairs beautifully with other parks on the Southern circuit, including Udzungwa National Park, Mikumi National Park and Nyerere National Park.

blocks.orig: Travel Tips from our experts about Ruaha

My name is Chengo, and I am a guide at Ruaha National Park for 18 years. Most of our guests are amazed by the number of elephants that they can see here! Also bird watchers can’t get enough of this park. And the beautiful landscape with its rivers and baobab trees is very pretty.
blocks.html: I'm Chengo, and I have guided in Ruaha National Park for 18 years. The sheer number of elephants you can see here astonishes most of our guests, and birdwatchers never tire of this park either. Add the lovely scenery of rivers and baobab trees and you have a very pretty place indeed.

blocks.orig: Don’t spend less than 2 days here. The distance is big, and the park is worth a longer visit!
blocks.html: Plan at least 2 days here. It is a long way to come, and the park deserves a longer stay!

blocks.orig: The road to Ruaha is passable throughout the year. Ruaha National Park has a bimodal pattern of rain forest; the short rainfall season begins November (February is best time for bird watching!), while the long season is between April to May. The national park experiences its dry season between June and October.
blocks.html: The road into Ruaha can be used all year round. Ruaha National Park has two rainy seasons: the short rains start in November (February is the top month for birdwatching!), while the long rains fall from April to May. The dry season in the park runs from June to October.

blocks.orig: Ruaha National Park is mainly characterized by its many acacias baobab trees. It is best known for its large elephant population, which is the most concentrated population in Africa! With a bit of luck, you may also see the endangered wild dogs!
blocks.html: Acacias and the many baobab trees give Ruaha National Park its distinctive look. The park is famous above all for its large elephant population, the densest in Africa! And with some luck you may spot the endangered wild dogs too!
